In the chemical formula of an ionic compound, the positively charged cations appear before the negatively charged anions. The name of an ionic compound consists of the cation's name followed by the anion's name.

content.text: The name of a monatomic (single-atom) cation is the same as the name of the element. For metals that can form more than one cation, the cation's charge is written as a Roman numeral after the element name.

pieces.text: Group 1 and 2 metals, aluminum, zinc, and silver tend to only form one cation. For example, the
cation is called a sodium ion.
Most other metals, many of which are transition metals, can form more than one cation. For example, the
cation is called an iron(III) ion.
The name of a monatomic anion consists of the root of the element name followed by the suffix "-ide." For example, the
anion is called a chloride ion.

Cations and anions can be polyatomic, containing multiple atoms, or monatomic, containing only one atom. The name of an ionic compound consists of the cation's name followed by the anion's name.
